seoTitle: Loudness Normalizer: Set Audio to a LUFS Target
metaDescription: Measure integrated loudness (LUFS) and set an audio file to -16, -14 or -23 LUFS with peak protection. Standard BS.1770 / EBU R128 method, in your browser.
intro: Measures the integrated loudness of an audio file in LUFS and applies the gain needed to reach a target, with a peak ceiling so the result does not clip.
why:
Peak normalising makes a file reach 0 dB at its loudest instant, which says little about how loud it sounds. Loudness in LUFS is a better match for what people hear, and broadcasters and streaming services use it to level programmes.

The measurement follows ITU-R BS.1770-4: a K-weighting filter, 400 ms blocks with 75 percent overlap, an absolute gate at -70 LUFS and a relative gate 10 LU below the average. We checked it against ffmpeg's ebur128 filter and it agrees to the tenth of a LU. The true peak value is an estimate from 4x cubic oversampling, not a certified meter.
howTo: Enter the target LUFS and the peak ceiling.
Pick what to do when peaks would exceed the ceiling: reduce the gain, limit the peaks or allow clipping.
Press Run and download the WAV, or tick "only measure" to read the loudness.

faq.a: EBU R128 broadcast uses -23 LUFS. Streaming services and podcast platforms publish their own values, often between -14 and -16. Check the current guidance of the service you upload to.
It applies a simple look-ahead limiter so no sample goes above the ceiling while keeping the loudness target. It is not a mastering limiter; heavy limiting can change the sound.

faq.q: Why did I not reach the target?
faq.a: With "reduce gain", the tool lowers the gain to keep peaks under the ceiling. Use "limit peaks" to get closer to the target.
Up to six channels are read as L R C LFE Ls Rs with the BS.1770 weights. Most files are mono or stereo.
